scene: Child: (looking at the tablet with the parent pointing at the screen)
Parent: "When they say go, then you can choose that one."
Child: (nods, continuing to look at the tablet screen)
Child: (looks intrigued, shifts slightly)
Parent: "Oh."
Child: "Oh." (still looking at the tablet, starts to move hand slightly)
Child: (continues to move hand towards the screen)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: "Yeah." (touches the screen)
Child: (turns to look at the parent)
Parent: "Wish ball."
Child: (smiles, looking engaged with the parent)
Child: (still looking at and interacting with the parent)

Parent: "Want to start the go pro cameras first? So you press this button here, and then you see these. If you see D, you match the time, and then it's good. Okay. Good. And also you can hold it. You can put it on this stand. Just do it in the way that is most comfortable to you. Yeah, we can start now."
Child: (nods, smiles, and looks ready to follow the instructions given by the parent)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: All right. You want to pick a book? One evening, after thinking it over for some time, Harold decided to go for a walk in the moonlight. Where's Harold?
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: He made a long, straight path so he wouldn't get lost. How's he making a path? What is he using?
Child: (pointing to the screen)
Parent: A crayon.
Child: (smiling)
Parent: A crayon. And he set off on his walk, taking his big purple crayon with him. What's that up there?
Child: (looks up at the parent)
Parent: Moon.
Child: (nods slightly)

Parent: Moon. But he didn't seem to be getting anywhere on the long, straight path. So he left the path for a shortcut across the field, and the moon went with him. The shortcut was led right to where Harold thought the forest ought to be. Is he drawing that?
Child: (nods affirmatively)
Parent: Yeah.
Child: (looking at the tablet with slight curiosity and finger in mouth)
Parent: What is it?
Child: (still looking at the tablet, finger in mouth, relaxed)
Parent: Tree.
Child: (continues to focus on the tablet while listening)
Parent: A tree? He didn't want to get lost in the woods, so he made a very small forest with just one tree in it. It turned out to be...
Child: (seems engaged and continues to look at the tablet)
Parent: Apple tree.
Child: (looking at the tablet, appearing interested)

Parent: "An apple tree. It looks good. The apples would be very tasty, Harold thought, when they got red. So he put a frightening dragon under the tree to guard the apples. Could you draw that? Why did he put the dragon there?"
Child: (thinking, then responding with hand gesture)
Parent: (nodding and looking at the child)
Child: "Because he doesn't want people to eat one."
Child: (looking at the tablet and making a hand gesture as if scared)

Parent: (smiling and pointing at the tablet) "Yeah, he doesn't want other people to come and get the apples. That's right. It was a terribly frightening dragon. It even frightened Harold, so he backed away. He got scared of his own dragon, huh? His hand holding the purple crayon shook. Suddenly, he realized what was happening. What did he draw with the crayon?"
Child: (smiling and thinking, then responding)
Parent: (listening attentively and encouraging the child)
Child: "Waves."
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen and looking curious)
Parent: "Waves. He made water. But by then, Harold was over his head and the ocean. He came up thinking fast. What's he going to draw?"
Child: (still looking at the tablet screen, intrigued)
Child: (continues to focus on the tablet screen)
Parent: "Boat."
Child: "A boat."
Parent: "And in no time, he was climbing aboard a little boat. He quickly set sail. And the moon sailed along with him."
Child: (lifts hand to mouth, thinking)
Child: (watching the tablet screen intensely)

Parent: "After he sailed long enough, Harold made land without much trouble. He stepped ashore on the beach, wondering where he was. The sandy beach reminded Harold of the picnics, and the thought of picnics made him... Do you know what that word is? Try to sound it out."
Child: "Hunjer."
Child: (looking at the screen and attempting to read)
Parent: (encouragingly guiding the child)
Child: "Hunjer."
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "The Y makes an E sound. Gree. Yep, hun-"
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, paying attention)
Parent: "Hungry."
Child: (nodding slightly, still attentive)
Child: (engaged, looking attentively at the tablet)

Parent: "Hungry, good. So he laid out a nice, simple picnic lunch. There was nothing but... What's that? Mm-hm (affirmative), pie. He's just eating pie. Made lots of pies. But they were all nine kinds of pie that Harold liked best. He liked nine different kinds of pie. What's your favorite kind of pie?"
Child: (smiling, looking curious)
Child: (turning head slightly toward the parent)
Parent: (looking at child expectantly)
Child: "Grape?"
Child: (looking at the parent, showing curiosity)
Parent: "Grape pie? I don't think I've ever tried grape pie."
Child: (looking down at the tablet, appearing thoughtful)
Parent: "Well, I never actually tried that before, either."
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet, hand on chin)
Parent: "It just sounds good?"
Child: (nodding slightly)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (seeming to ponder, one hand still on chin)
Parent: "What kind of pies have you tried that you liked the best?"
Child: (shrugging slightly)
Parent: "I don't know."
Child: (looking at the book and touching his face)
Parent: "When Harold finished his picnic, there was quite a lot left. He couldn't eat all of it, right? What do you think he's going to do next? Okay, let's find out."
Child: (continues looking at the book and follows along attentively)
Parent: "He hated to see so much delicious pie go to waste. So Harold left a very hungry moose and a deserving porcupine to finish it up. Where's the moose?"
Child: (points to the screen)
Parent: "Good. Where's the porcupine?"
Child: (points to the screen)

Parent: "Yep. And off he went, looking for a hill to climb to see where he was. Harold knew that the higher up you went, the farther he could see, so he decided to make the hill into a... What's bigger than a hill? Can you read that word?"
Child: (looks at the screen and starts reading)
Parent: (points to the word on the screen)
Child: (begins to sound out the word) "Mou..."
Parent: (nods encouragingly)
Child: (continues to sound out the word) "Tin. Mou..."
Parent: (smiles and watches attentively)
Child: "Tin."
Parent: "What is it?"
Child: "Mountain."
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged in the story)

Parent: "Good. If he went high enough, he thought he could see the window of his bedroom. He was tired, and he felt like he ought to be getting to bed. He hoped he could see his bedroom window from the top of the mountain. He's going up, up, up. But as he looked down over the other side, he slipped. Uh oh. And there wasn't any other side of the mountain. He was falling in thin air, but luckily he kept his wits and his purple crayon. What do you think he's going to draw while he's falling?"
Child: (thinks for a moment) "A parachute?"
Parent: "A what?"
Child: "A parachute?"

Parent: "Yeah, that's a good idea. He decided to do something else. He made a balloon, and he grabbed onto it, a big balloon. Parachute would have been a good idea, too. And he made a basket under the balloon big enough to stand in, like a hot air balloon. Have you seen those? Balloons that float up in the sky? He had a fine view from the balloon, but he couldn't see his window. He couldn't even see a house, so he made a house with windows, and he landed the balloon on the grass in the front yard. None of the windows was his window. He tried to think where his window ought to be. We made some more windows. He made a big building full of windows. He made lots of big buildings full of windows."
Child: "That's a city."
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged)
Parent: "It's a city, yeah. He made a whole city full of windows, but none of the windows was his window."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He couldn't think where it might be. He decided to ask a policemen."
Child: (continues to pay attention to the tablet)
Parent: "The policemen pointed the way Harold was going anyway, but Harold thanked him, and he walked along with the moon, wishing he was in his room and in bed."
Child: (observing the imagery on the tablet)
Parent: "Then suddenly, Harold remembered. He remembered where his bedroom window was when there was a moon. It was always right around the moon."
Child: (interested, looking towards the parent’s direction)
Parent: "And then Harold made his bed. He got in, and he drew up the covers."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "The purple crayon dropped on the floor, and Harold dropped off. Can you read those last two words?"
Child: (looking closely at the tablet)
Parent: "To sleep."
Child: "To sleep."
Parent: "To sleep, good. The end. That was a fun story. I think if you tap there, you can go back to the bookshelf."
Child: (leans closer to the tablet)
Parent: "Choose another book. I think we can go like this and see more books, too."
Child: (scans the bookshelf on the tablet)
Parent: "Is there one of these you want? Harry the dirty dog?"
Child: "Yeah."
Parent: "Harry was a white dog with black spots who liked everything except... What's that say? What did he not like? With the G?"
Child: (leans toward the tablet, examining it)
Parent: "What G?"
Child: (looks at the tablet, concentrating on the storybook)
Parent: "Right here, this word here. Get... After the three dots. Dot, dot, dot. He liked everything except what? Can you read that part?"
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet, attempts to read)
Parent: (points at the specific word on the tablet)
Child: "Get... Gilt... Get..."
Parent: "Do you know what I-N-G... It's close, yeah. Do you know what sound I-N-G makes at the end of a word? Ing. Can you say ing? So what's that word?"
Child: (tries to concentrate, sounding out the word)
Parent: (patiently points at the word again)
Child: "Getting."
Parent: (smiles, nods encouragingly)
Child: (smiles back, feeling accomplished)
Child: (seated, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Getting, yep. He liked everything except getting what? A... getting a...
Child: (engaged, looking at the tablet)
Child: (leaning forward, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Bat.
Parent: Do you remember what T-H together, what sound that makes? Bath.
Child: (still leaning forward, looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting more upright, looking at the parent)
Parent: Bath.
Parent: Yeah, so he liked everything except what?
Child: (starts to lean forward)
Child: (leaning close to the tablet again)
Parent: Bath.
Child: (bending over, looking closely at the tablet)
Parent: "Yep. So one day, he heard the water running in the tub. So he took the scrubbing brush, and what did he do? What did he do with the scrub brush for his bath? Did he like baths?"
Child: "No."

Parent: "So what do you think he's going to do with the brush for his bath? He buried it in the backyard. Then he ran away from home. He played where they were fixing the street and got very dirty. He played at the railroad and got even dirtier. You see him? Where did he go?"
Child: "Railroad."
Parent: "I don't see him. Where's the dog?"
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Oh, there he is. Yeah. He played tag with the other dogs and became dirtier still. He slid down a coal shoot and got the dirtiest of all. In fact, he changed. He changed from a white dog with black spots to a black dog with white spots. How come he was the black dog now?"
Child: "Because he got dirty."
Child: (looking at the tablet, standing up)
Parent: "Because he was so dirty. Although there were many other things to do, Harry began to wonder if his family thought that he had really run away."
Child: (looking at the tablet, standing up)
Parent: "He felt tired and hungry, too. So without stopping on the way, he ran back home."
Child: (looking at the tablet, standing up)
Parent: "When Harry got to his house, he crawled through the fence and sat looking at the back door."
Child: (looking at the tablet, standing up)
Parent: "One of the family looked out and said, 'There's a strange dog in the backyard. By the way, has anyone seen Harry?'"
Child: (looking at the tablet, standing up)
Parent: "Where's Harry?"
Child: "Right there."
Parent: "Right there, but can they recognize him?"
Child: "No."
Parent: "No, they don't know who it is. Why don't they know who he is?"
Child: "Because he got dirty."
Child: (watching the tablet with interest, looking at the parent)

Parent: Because he's so dirty. Yep. He looks different, huh? When Harry heard this, he tried very hard to show them that he was Harry. He started to do his old clever tricks. He flip flopped, and then he flop flipped, and he rolled over and played dead. He danced and sang. He did these tricks over and over again, but everyone shook their heads and said, "Oh no, it couldn't be Harry." Harry gave up and walked slowly toward the gate, but suddenly he stopped. He ran to a corner of the garden. What do you think he's going to do? He has an idea.
Child: (looks away from the tablet, turns slightly toward the parent)
Parent: Take a bath.
Child: (turning back towards the tablet)
Parent: Yeah. He ran to the corner of the garden and started to dig furiously. What's he digging for, do you think?
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: What did he hide? Do you remember?
Child: Bath.
Parent: Bath.
Child: (looking at the tablet screen)

Parent: "Yeah, the scrub brush for his bath. Soon, he jumped away from the hole, barking short, happy barks. He found the scrubbing brush, and carrying it in his mouth, he ran into the house, and up the stairs he dashed with the family close behind. He jumped into the bathtub and sat up, begging with the scrubbing brush in his mouth, a trick he certainly had never done before. "This little doggie wants a bath," cried the little girl, and her father said, "Why don't you and your brother give him one?" Harry's bath was the soapiest one he'd ever had. It worked like magic. As soon as the children started to scrub, they began shouting, "Mommy, daddy, look, come quick." Do you think they recognize him now?"
Child: "Yeah."

Parent: ""It's Harry, it's Harry," they cried. Harry wagged his tail and was very, very happy. His family combed and brushed him lovingly, and he became, once again, a white dog with black spots. Do you think you can read that first sentence? You want to try it? What's the first word? I-T. Okay. It was wonderful to be home. After dinner, Harry fell asleep in his favorite place, happily dreaming of how much fun it had been getting dirty. He slept so soundly. He didn't even feel the scrubbing brush he'd hidden under his pillow. Do you see it?"
Child: "Yeah."
Parent: "Where is it? Right there. Yeah. He still doesn't like baths, huh? That was fun. Do you want to try this one?"
Child: (smiling, still looking at the tablet screen)
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "Okay."
Child: (nodding slightly, showing interest)
Child: (looks thoughtful, still focused on the tablet)
Parent: "What do you think this story's going to be about? Congratulations. Today is your day. You're off to great places. You're off and away."
Child: (keeping attention on the tablet, seems engaged)
Child: (turns slightly away from the tablet, appears hesitant)
Parent: "I want you to read it, not me. Because I don't really like-"
Child: (starts to look away from the tablet)
Child: (turning fully away from the tablet)

Parent: "You don't want to read it? Okay. You want me to read it? You have brains in your head, and you have feet in your shoes. You can steer yourself any direction you choose. You're on your own, and you know what you know, and you are the guy who will decide where to go. Try not to bump the table. That shakes the camera a little bit."
Child: (sits back down, facing towards the tablet but not looking directly)
Child: (looking at the book)
Parent: "You'll look up and down streets, look them over with care. About some, you will say,"
Child: (looking at the book)
Parent: ""I don't choose to go there with your head full of brains and your shoes full of feet, you're too smart to go down any not so good street. Would you go down that street?"
Child: "No."
Parent: "No, I wouldn't either. What street would you go? Choose here? Yeah, that one looks better to me, too. Why wouldn't you go down that one?"
Child: "Just because it has crocodiles."
Parent: "Yeah, it looks dangerous, huh? And you may not find any you'll want to go down. In that case, of course, you'll head straight out of town. Sometimes you can just leave, right?"
Child: "Yeah."
Child: (looking at the tablet, slightly leaning towards the parent)

Parent: "It's opener there in the wide open air. Out there things can happen and frequently due to people as brainy and footsy as you. And when things start to happen, don't worry, don't Stew. Just go right along. You'll start happening too. Wow. Oh, the places you'll go. You'll be on your way up. You'll be seeing great sights. You'll join the high flyers who soar to high heights. What's he riding?"
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet)
Parent: "A parachute?"
Child: (slightly looking up at the parent)
Parent: "What is it? It's just like..."
Child: (turns back to look at the tablet)
Parent: "Hot air balloon?"
Child: (nods slightly, still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Yeah, hot air balloon, good. You won't lag behind because you'll have the speed. You'll pass the whole gang, and you'll soon take the lead. Wherever you fly, you'll be the best of the best. Wherever you go, you'll top all the rest. Except when you don't because sometimes, you won't. I'm sorry to say so, but sadly, it's true that bang ups and hang ups can happen to you. You can get all hung up in a prickly perch, and your gang will fly on, and you'll be left in a lurch."
Parent: (pauses and looks at child)
Parent: "Does that happen sometimes to you? Do you always win every game that you play? How does it make you feel when you don't win?"
Child: (looks up at the parent)
Child: "Well, I... like just... I don't know."
Child: (looking at the tablet, arms on the table)

Parent: "You don't know? I know you don't like it when you don't win, but it's okay sometimes, right? It happens to everybody, like this guy, too. He was doing great, but then he got stuck on a tree, huh? It's okay if sometimes we don't win. You can still have fun, right?"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, nodding)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (keeping eyes on the tablet, seeming more engaged)

Parent: "You'll come down from the lurch with an unpleasant bump, and the chances are then that you'll be in a slump. And sometimes things don't work out for us the way we want them to. How do you think he feels now?"
Child: (thinking, looking at the parent momentarily)
Parent: "Sad."
Child: (looking back at the tablet, more relaxed)
Parent: (smiling at the child)
Child: (sitting and closely looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Yeah, he's probably a little sad, but guess what? It's going to be okay. When you're in a slump, you're not in for much fun. Un-slumping yourself is not easily done. It's hard when you feel sad, right? But you will come to a place where the streets are not marked. Some windows are lighted, but most of them dark. A place you could sprain both your elbow and chin. How dare you stay out? Do you dare to go in? Oh, do you dare to stay out? Do you dare to go in? How much can you lose? How much can you win? Sometimes you don't know. Should you try it anyway? Even if you don't know, should you try? You don't know. And if you go in, should you turn left or right or right in three quarters or maybe not quite? Or go around back and sneak in from behind? Simple it's not, I'm afraid you will find, for a mind maker upper to make up his mind."
Child: (listening intently, occasionally glancing at the parent)
Child: (raising a hand to mouth, looking thoughtful)

Parent: "You can get so confused that you'll start in to race down long wiggled roads at a break necking pace and grind on for miles across weirdish wild space, headed, I fear, toward a most useless place. The waiting place. For people just waiting, waiting for a train to go, or a bus to come, or a plane to go, or the mail to come, or the rain to go, or the phone to ring, or the snow to snow, or waiting around for a yes or a no, or a waiting for their hair to grow. Everyone is just... what? Waiting."
Child: (whispering) "Waiting."
Parent: "Waiting."
Child: (appears contemplative, maintains focus on the tablet)

Parent: "Waiting, yeah. Waiting for the fish to bite, or waiting for when to fly a kite, or waiting around for a Friday night, or waiting perhaps for their uncle Jake or a pot to boil or a better break or a string of pearls or a pair of pants or a wig with curls or another chance. Everyone is just waiting, but that's not for you. Somehow you'll escape all that waiting and staying. You'll find the bright places where boom bands are playing. With banner flip flapping once more, you'll ride high, ready for anything under the sky, ready because you're that kind of guy."
Child: (continues to listen attentively while fidgeting a little)

Parent: "Oh, the places you'll go! There is fun to be done. There are points to be scored. There are games to be won, and the magical things you can do with that ball will make you the winningest winner of all. Fame! You'll be famous as famous can be, with the whole wide world watching you win on TV. Except when they don't because sometimes, they won't. I'm afraid that sometimes, you'll play lonely games, too. Games you can't win because you'll play against you. All alone, whether you like it or not, alone will be something you'll be quite a lot. Sometimes you'll be alone. And when you're alone, there's a very good chance you'll meet things that scare you right out of your pants. There's some down the road between hither and yon that can scare you so much, you won't want to go on. You get scared sometimes? What's scary for you?"
Child: (breaking eye contact with the tablet, looks at the parent)
Child: "Being alone just..."
Child: (Sitting and looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Being alone, yeah. I think that's scary for a lot of people. But on you will go, though the weather be foul. On you will go, though your enemies prowl."
Child: (Continues looking at the tablet, listening)

Parent: "On you will go, though the hacken cracks howl. Onward up many a frightening creek, though your arms may get sore and your sneakers may leak. On and on you will hike, and I know you'll hike far and face up to your problems, whatever they are."
Child: (Leaning on the table, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "That's a big thing. You'll get mixed up, of course, as you already know. You'll get mixed up with many strange birds as you go."
Child: "Oh, where is that guy running?"
Parent: (Engaged, looks at the tablet)
Child: (Pointing to the tablet, seems curious)
Parent: "I don't know. So be sure when you step, step with care."
Child: (Focuses back on the tablet)
Parent: "Yep, there he is. And great tact and remember that life's a great balancing act. Just never forget to be dextrous and deft, and never mix up your right foot with your left."
Child: (Gazing at the tablet, listening attentively)
Parent: "Where's your right foot? Do you know where your right foot? Where's your right foot?"
Child: (Points to one foot)
Parent: "Do you remember? That's your left foot. That's your right foot."
Child: (Looking down at their feet, seeming to remember)
Parent: "Yep, good job. What's this one?"
Child: "Left."
Child: (Pointing confidently at their left foot)
Parent: "Left, good. And what's this one?"
Child: "Right."
Child: (sitting at the table with the tablet, looking slightly relaxed)
Parent: Right. And will you succeed? What do you think?
Child: (looks thoughtful, unsure)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet screen)
Child: (looks at the parent, still unsure)
Child: (turns head towards the parent, looks a bit puzzled)
Parent: I don't know what s-
Child: (leans back slightly in the chair, thinking)
Child: (looks back at the tablet, a bit more attentive)
Parent: Yes, you will indeed. Do you know what succeed means?
Child: (leans in towards the tablet, showing interest)
Parent: (points at the tablet screen again)
Child: (engaged with the tablet)
Parent: (sitting beside the child and watching the tablet alongside)
Child: "Thank you."
Parent: (gets up from the chair)
Child: "So now we'll take..."
Parent: (walks away from the table)
Child: (turns and watches the parent walking away)
Child: "Do you have a tissue in here we can grab?"
Parent: (standing away from the table)
Parent: "Maybe I can just take this off, [crosstalk 00:26:39] and then we have a restroom just outside. Thank you."
Parent: (continues to stand, near the child)
Child: (standing near the parent)
Child: "Okay. Do you have to keep these locked? [crosstalk 00:26:46]."
Parent: "Outside, do you see the two doors on the left? Yeah."
Child: (heads towards the indicated direction)
Parent: "Cute. Well, these are just [inaudible 00:27:03]."
(Tablet and chairs in view, the parent and child are now out of frame)
Parent: "[crosstalk 00:26:39] and then we have a restroom just outside. Thank you."
Child: (out of frame)
Parent: (out of frame)
Parent: "And those are to turn off the two go pros. Just, it's, oh, well. It seems something's wrong with this go pro. Just often automatically stops."

Parent: "But yeah, the go pro [inaudible 00:27:19]. So that's fine. It's harder to do [inaudible 00:27:25] and Tuesday, so today we'll have two videos. And always select parent and rotation review, so it's, yeah. [inaudible 00:27:33] And then do stuff you do. Oh, did you?"
Parent: "Oh, do I have to do it on the..."
Additional Voices: (associates out of frame)
Parent and Child: (remain out of frame)
Parent: "No, no, so we stopped videoing."
Additional Voices: "Yeah, this one [inaudible 00:27:55]."
